name: Near-Earth Satellites
tagline: The artificial shell — thousands of working spacecraft and debris fragments swarming low Earth orbit.
history: The dots swarming Earth are the newest feature of the planet — an artificial shell that did not exist before 1957, when Sputnik 1's beeps announced the space age. Low Earth orbit now hosts more than eleven thousand working satellites: Starlink and other mega-constellations beam internet from shells a few hundred kilometres up, weather and Earth-observation fleets watch the surface in polar orbits, and the ISS and Tiangong carry crews around the planet sixteen times a day. Sharing the same lanes is the debris record of seventy years — dead satellites, spent rocket stages and fragments from collisions like the 2009 Iridium–Kosmos impact and the 2007 anti-satellite test. Each fleck travels at roughly 8 km/s, fast enough that a paint chip can crater a window, which is why stations dodge tracked debris and engineers fear the Kessler cascade — collisions spawning fragments that spawn more collisions. The swarm is humanity's scaffolding: navigation, communications, climate science and every crewed mission begin inside this thin, crowded shell.
